Below is a short “one‑paper‑highlight” for each of several world‑renowned deep‑learning researchers. For every talent I list a single, highly‑influential paper (the one that is most often credited with shaping the field), a brief description of why it matters, and a link to the freely‑available version (arXiv or the publisher’s open‑access copy). | Researcher | Signature Paper (year) | Why It’s a “cutting‑edge” milestone | Key Contributions & Impact | Open‑Access Link | |------------|------------------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------|------------------| | **Geoffrey Hinton** | **“Learning Multiple Layers of Representation”** (2006) – *Trends in Cognitive Sciences* (also the 2006 **NIPS** tutorial “A Fast Learning Algorithm for Deep Belief Nets”) | First systematic demonstration that **deep belief networks (DBNs)** can be trained layer‑by‑layer using unsupervised pre‑training, making deep nets practical on real data. | • Introduced **contrastive divergence** for training Restricted Boltzmann Machines.
• Showed that unsupervised pre‑training dramatically reduces the amount of labeled data needed.
• Sparked the modern deep‑learning renaissance. | https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/DeepLearning.pdf | | **Yann LeCun** | **“Gradient‑Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition”** (1998) – *Proceedings of the IEEE* (LeNet‑5) | The **first successful convolutional neural network (CNN)** applied to a large‑scale real‑world task (handwritten digit recognition). | • Designed the **LeNet‑5** architecture (convolution → pooling → fully‑connected).
• Demonstrated back‑propagation works for spatially‑structured data.
• Laid the groundwork for today’s vision‑centric deep nets (AlexNet, ResNet, etc.). | https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/726791 | | **Yoshua Bengio** | **“Learning Long‑Term Dependencies with Gradient Descent is Difficult”** (1994) – *IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks* (co‑authored with Sepp Hochreiter) | Early identification of the **vanishing‑gradient problem**, which motivated the later invention of **LSTM** and other gated recurrent units. | • Formal analysis of why standard RNNs struggle with long‑range dependencies.
• Influenced the design of **Long Short‑Term Memory (LSTM)** (1997) and later **GRU**.
• Still cited in modern sequence‑modeling surveys. | https://doi.org/10.1109/72.279181 | | **Andrew Ng** | **“Sparse Autoencoder”** (2011) – *Proceedings of the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML)* (with J. D. Lee, M. A. Ranzato) | Popularized **unsupervised feature learning** for vision and speech, showing that a simple autoencoder with sparsity constraints can learn useful representations without labels. | • Demonstrated that deep unsupervised pre‑training can rival hand‑crafted features.
• Influenced the rise of **deep learning for speech recognition** (e.g., Google Voice Search).
• Served as a bridge between academic research and large‑scale industrial deployment (Google Brain, Baidu). | https://icml.cc/2011/papers/119.pdf | | **Demis Hassabis** (DeepMind) | **“Human‑level control through deep reinforcement learning”** (2015) – *Nature* (Mnih et al., Deep Q‑Network) | First **deep reinforcement‑learning (RL)** system (the DQN) that learned to play Atari 2600 games directly from raw pixels, matching or surpassing human performance on many titles. | • Combined **convolutional nets** with **Q‑learning** and experience replay.
• Showed that a single network can master multiple tasks without task‑specific engineering.
• Opened the floodgate for modern RL breakthroughs (AlphaGo, AlphaStar, MuZero). | https://www.nature.com/articles/nature14236 | | **Jürgen Schmidhuber** | **“Long Short‑Term Memory”** (1997) – *Neural Computation* (with Sepp Hochreiter) | The **LSTM** architecture solved the vanishing‑gradient problem for recurrent networks and became the de‑facto standard for sequence modeling. | • Introduced **gates** (input, forget, output) to control information flow.
• Enabled breakthroughs in language modeling, speech synthesis, and time‑series prediction.
• Basis for later models such as **Transformer‑XL** and **GPT**‑style language models. | https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1997.9.8.1735 | | **Ian Goodfellow** | **“Generative Adversarial Nets”** (2014) – *NeurIPS* (with Jean Pouget‑Abadie, Mehdi Mirza, et al.) | Introduced **GANs**, a new paradigm for generative modeling that pits a generator against a discriminator in a minimax game. | • Sparked an explosion of research on image synthesis, style transfer, and unsupervised representation learning.
• Led to variants such as **DCGAN**, **WGAN**, **StyleGAN**, and countless applications in art, data augmentation, and simulation. | https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2661 | | **Fei-Fei Li** | **“ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks”** (2012) – *NeurIPS* (AlexNet, co‑authored with Alex Krizhevsky & Sutskever) | Though the first author is Krizhevsky, Fei‑Fei Li’s leadership of the **ImageNet** project made the dataset possible; the paper demonstrated that deep CNNs can achieve **human‑level accuracy** on a massive visual benchmark. | • Popularized **ReLU**, **dropout**, and **GPU‑accelerated training**.
• Triggered the “AlexNet moment” that launched modern computer‑vision deep learning.
• Set the stage for subsequent architectures (VGG, ResNet, EfficientNet). | https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2012/hash/c399862d3b9d6b76c8436e924a68c45b-Abstract.html | ### How to Use These Papers 1. **Read the abstract & introduction** to grasp the problem the authors were solving. 2. **Study the model architecture diagrams** (most of these papers include clear visualizations). 3. **Check the experimental section** for datasets, training tricks, and evaluation metrics—many of these tricks (e.g., dropout, experience replay) are still standard today. 4. **Look at the citations** (Google Scholar “Cited by”) to see how the community built on the work; this often points you to the next‑generation “cutting‑edge” papers. **USD → EUR Exchange‑Rate Summary (Jan 1 – Mar 31 2023)**  

| Date (2023) | USD → EUR Rate* | % Change vs. Prior Date |
|-------------|----------------|--------------------------|
| Jan 1       | **0.945**      | –                        |
| Feb 1       | **0.925**      | **‑2.12 %** |
| Mar 1       | **0.935**      | **+1.08 %** |
| Mar 31      | **0.915**      | **‑2.14 %** |
| **Overall (Jan 1 → Mar 31)** | **0.915** | **‑3.17 %** |

\*Rate = 1 USD = X EUR (rounded to three decimal places).

### How many euros for a USD 10,000 conversion?

Using the most recent rate on **31 Mar 2023 (0.915 EUR per USD)**:

\[
10{,}000\ \text{USD} \times 0.915\ \frac{\text{EUR}}{\text{USD}} = \boxed{9{,}150\ \text{EUR}}
\]

If the client were to convert the amount at the **average rate** over the period (average of the four rates = (0.945 + 0.925 + 0.935 + 0.915)/4 = 0.930), the conversion would be:

\[
10{,}000 \times 0.930 = 9{,}300\ \text{EUR}
\]

### Key Take‑aways for the Client

1. **Gradual weakening** of the euro against the dollar over the quarter – the USD bought about **3.2 % more euros** on Mar 31 than on Jan 1.  
2. The **largest single‑month swing** was the drop from Jan 1 to Feb 1 (‑2.12 %).  
3. A conversion on the last day of the period would yield **9,150 EUR**, whereas using the quarter‑average rate would give **9,300 EUR** – a difference of **150 EUR** (≈1.6 %).  

Feel free to let me know if you need a visual chart, a deeper dive into daily rates, or scenario analysis for other conversion dates.

inference_output.content:
**Step 1 – Identify the currency with the lowest EUR‑exchange rate**

From the rates we retrieved:

| Currency | EUR‑exchange rate (EUR per unit) |
|----------|----------------------------------|
| USD      | 0.92 → 0.93 → 0.91 |
| JPY      | 0.0071 → 0.0072 → 0.0070 |
| GBP      | 1.15 → 1.14 → 1.13 |

The **Japanese yen (JPY)** has the smallest value (0.0070 EUR per JPY on 20 Jan 2025).

---

**Step 2 – Convert 5 000 JPY to euros**

Using the JPY → EUR rate for the same day (20 Jan 2025 = 0.0070 EUR/JPY):

\[
5 000\ \text{JPY} \times 0.0070\ \frac{\text{EUR}}{\text{JPY}} = 35.0\ \text{EUR}
\]

---

**Step 3 – Convert those euros to US dollars (the “initial exchange combination” was USD ↔ EUR)**  

The USD → EUR rate on 20 Jan 2025 is 0.91 EUR per USD, i.e.  

\[
1\ \text{USD} = 0.91\ \text{EUR} \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; 1\ \text{EUR} = \frac{1}{0.91}\ \text{USD} \approx 1.0989\ \text{USD}
\]

Now convert the 35 EUR:

\[
35.0\ \text{EUR} \times \frac{1}{0.91}\ \frac{\text{USD}}{\text{EUR}} \approx 35.0 \times 1.0989 = 38.46\ \text{USD}
\]

---

### Result
- **5000 JPY** → **35 EUR** → **≈ 38.5 USD**

So, using the lowest‑rate currency (JPY) and the original USD/EUR pair, 5 000 yen would purchase **about 38.5 US dollars** (rounded to two decimal places).

The averages are weighted‑means: each age is multiplied by its share of the population, summed, and then divided by 100 % (the percentages add to 100 % for every group).

\[
\frac{5\!\times\!8 + 15\!\times\!18 + 25\!\times\!25 + 35\!\times\!30 + 45\!\times\!19}{100}
= \frac{2{,}840}{100}=28.4\text{ years}
\]

The same weighted‑average formula was applied to each of the other five groups.

### Quick take‑away  

- **Males** named Emma, Olivia, and Ava tend to be older on average than females with the same name (≈ 2–4 years older).  
- The **largest gender gap** appears for **Emma** (≈ 3.8 years).  
- All three names show a modest shift toward younger ages for females, reflecting the higher percentages of the younger‑age brackets in the female distributions.

**COVID‑19 Mortality (Deaths ÷ Confirmed Cases) – United States vs. Brazil**  

| Country | Confirmed cases | Deaths | Mortality rate* |
|---------|----------------|--------|-----------------|
| United States (US) | 50,000,000 | 800,000 | **1.60 %** |
| Brazil (BR) | 30,000,000 | 600,000 | **2.00 %** |

\*Mortality rate = (Deaths ÷ Confirmed cases) × 100.  

### What the numbers mean
* **United States:** About 1.6 deaths for every 100 confirmed infections.  
* **Brazil:** About 2.0 deaths for every 100 confirmed infections.  

### Comparison
* Brazil’s COVID‑19 mortality rate is roughly **0.4 percentage points higher** than that of the United States, representing a **~25 % higher** fatality proportion relative to confirmed cases.

Data on hepatitis B virus in the United States can be obtained from multiple official sources. Different data indicators reflect the prevalence, prevention, and control of hepatitis B in the population:

### Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
1. **Incidence data**: The CDC collects information on the incidence of hepatitis B through a national surveillance system. According to CDC data, the incidence of acute hepatitis B in the United States has generally shown a downward trend in recent years. Over the past few decades, with the widespread implementation of the hepatitis B vaccination program, the incidence of acute hepatitis B has decreased significantly. For example, before the vaccine was widely available, more than 200,000 cases of acute hepatitis B were reported each year. By around 2020, the incidence of acute hepatitis B had dropped to approximately 1.5 cases per 100,000 people.
2. **Infection rate data**: The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) conducted in the United States samples different age and ethnic groups to estimate the prevalence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (i.e., the chronic hepatitis B virus infection rate). The data shows that the overall prevalence of HBsAg in the United States is approximately 0.6%, but the proportion is higher in some specific high-risk groups. For instance, the prevalence of HBsAg among Asian Americans is about 5% - 10%, several times that of the general population. This is mainly because many Asian immigrants come from regions with a high prevalence of hepatitis B, and household transmission is relatively common.
3. **Mortality data**: The CDC records hepatitis B-related deaths through the death registration system. The hepatitis B-related mortality rate has also changed over time. In recent years, the number of deaths due to hepatitis B-related diseases has ranged from several hundred to over a thousand per year. Hepatitis B-related deaths are mainly due to the progression of the disease to severe complications such as liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.

### Other data sources
1. **Hospital and healthcare system data**: Large hospitals and healthcare networks record information on hepatitis B patients they admit, including patient diagnoses and treatment. Although these data are local, they can provide more detailed clinical information, such as the effectiveness of different treatment methods and the length of patient hospital stays. Some academic medical centers also conduct research projects on hepatitis B, collecting more in-depth clinical and research data.
2. **Research data from scientific research institutions**: Research projects on hepatitis B carried out by universities and professional medical research institutions collect data on specific populations or research questions. These studies may involve aspects such as the molecular biological characteristics of the hepatitis B virus and clinical trials of new treatment regimens. Their data can provide cutting-edge scientific evidence for the prevention and control of hepatitis B.

For instance, the prevalence of HBsAg among Asian Americans is about 5% - 10%, several times that of the general population. This is mainly because many Asian immigrants come from regions with a high prevalence of hepatitis B, and household transmission is relatively common.
3. **Mortality data**: The CDC records hepatitis B-related deaths through the death registration system. The hepatitis B-related mortality rate has also changed over time. In recent years, the number of deaths due to hepatitis B-related diseases has ranged from several hundred to over a thousand per year. Hepatitis B-related deaths are mainly due to the progression of the disease to severe complications such as liver cirrhosis and liver cancer.

These studies may involve aspects such as the molecular biological characteristics of the hepatitis B virus and clinical trials of new treatment regimens. ---

## 1. Logical  
**Part of Speech:** *Adjective*  

**Definition:**  
*In accordance with logic; reasonable; sensible.*

**Example Sentences:**  
1. His argument was **logical** and well‑structured.  
2. It is **logical** to assume that the sun will rise tomorrow.  
3. The decision was based on **logical** reasoning.  
4. She provided a **logical** explanation for her actions.  
5. The solution to the problem was both simple and **logical**.  

---

## 2. Reasonable  
**Part of Speech:** *Adjective*  

**Definition:**  
*Fair; sensible; justifiable.*

**Example Sentences:**  
1. It is **reasonable** to expect that prices will rise.  
2. She made a **reasonable** argument for her case.  
3. The request was considered **reasonable** by the committee.  
4. He offered a **reasonable** explanation for his actions.  
5. The price of the car was **reasonable** given its condition.  

---  

These entries satisfy the original request for **definitions and example sentences** for each synonym of the third synonym (“rational”).

*Overall*: Vehicle traffic is moderately congested, mainly due to the accident on Avenida da Liberdade. Public‑transport flow is smooth, and pedestrian movement is unaffected.

---

**Parking Availability – Downtown Lisbon (within 500 m radius)**  

| Parking Lot | Distance from centre (m) | Total Spaces | Available Spaces | Availability % |
|-------------|--------------------------|--------------|------------------|----------------|

| **Rossio** | 300 m | 100 | 10 | 10 % |

*Key take‑aways*  

- **Praça dos Restauradores** offers the most open spots (50 spaces) and is the closest option.  
- **Avenida da Liberdade** still has some capacity but is more limited (20 spaces).  
- **Rossio** is the most constrained (only 10 spaces left).  

---

### Recommendations for Your Afternoon Trip

1. **Route Planning**  
   - To avoid the medium‑level congestion on Avenida da Liberdade, consider taking **Rua da Prata** or **Rua Augusta** as alternative north‑south corridors.  
   - If you’re using a navigation app, set it to “avoid traffic incidents” – it will automatically reroute around the accident zone.

2. **Parking Choice**  
   - **Best option:** Drive to **Praça dos Restauradores** (100 m away). It has the highest availability and is centrally located for most downtown attractions.  
   - If you prefer a spot closer to the main shopping stretch on Avenida da Liberdade, be prepared for limited space (20 spots) and possibly a short walk from the lot.

3. **Timing**  
   - Arriving **just after 5 pm** may give you a better chance of finding a spot before the accident‑related slowdown builds up.  
   - If you can delay arrival until after **6 pm**, the traffic congestion remains at the same level, but the accident area may be cleared, improving flow on Avenida da Liberdade.

4. **Alternative Transport**  
   - Given the low congestion for public transport, you could also consider taking a tram (e.g., **Tram 28**) or a bus to the downtown core and park at a peripheral garage (e.g., **Parque de Estacionamento do Campo Grande**) then walk or use a short ride‑share.

Feel free to let me know if you need a detailed route map, real‑time updates closer to your departure, or information on any specific parking garages beyond the three listed. Safe travels!

**Teaching Pack – “Resilience”**

---

## 1. Detailed Definition  

| Part of Speech | Definition | Source |
|----------------|------------|--------|
| **noun** | **1.** *The capacity to recover quickly from difficulties; toughness.* | (Merriam‑Webster) |
| | **2.** *The ability of a substance or object to spring back into shape; elasticity.* | (Merriam‑Webster) |

*Key ideas to stress for learners:*  
- **Psychological/Emotional resilience** – bouncing back after setbacks, stress, or trauma.  
- **Physical/Material resilience** – how a material returns to its original form after being deformed (e.g., rubber, steel).  

---

## 2. Example Sentences  

| # | Sentence | Context |
|---|----------|---------|
| 1 | *Her **resilience** in the face of adversity is admirable.* | Personal/character trait |
| 2 | *The **resilience** of the material makes it ideal for use in construction.* | Engineering/materials |
| 3 | *Children often show remarkable **resilience** to change.* | Developmental psychology |
| 4 | *After the hurricane, the community’s **resilience** helped them rebuild faster than expected.* | Social/community |
| 5 | *A rubber band demonstrates **resilience** because it snaps back after being stretched.* | Everyday illustration |

Feel free to ask students to create their own sentences or to match each sentence with the appropriate meaning (psychological vs. material).

---

## 3. Pronunciation  

| Audio Format | Link (click to play) |
|--------------|----------------------|
| **MP3** | <https://example.com/pronunciation/resilience.mp3> |
| **WAV** | <https://example.com/pronunciation/resilience.wav> |

**Phonetic transcription (IPA):** /rɪˈzɪl.jəns/  

*Teaching tip:* Play the MP3, have students repeat, then break the word into syllables: re‑sil‑i‑ence. Emphasize the stress on the second syllable (**‑ZIL‑**).

---

## 4. Visual Resources  

| # | Description | Image Type | Link |
|---|-------------|------------|------|
| 1 | *A plant growing through a crack in the pavement* – symbolises life persisting despite obstacles. | Photo | <https://example.com/images/resilience1.jpg> |
| 2 | *A person climbing a mountain, symbolizing overcoming challenges* – visual metaphor for personal resilience. | Photo | <https://example.com/images/resilience2.jpg> |
| 3 | *A rubber band returning to its original shape after being stretched* – illustrates material resilience. | Photo | <https://example.com/images/resilience3.jpg> |

You can embed these images in a slide deck or print them as hand‑outs. Ask learners to write a short caption linking each picture to one of the definitions.

---

## 5. Quick Classroom Activity Ideas  

| Activity | How to Use the Materials |
|----------|--------------------------|
| **Definition Matching** | Provide cards with the two definitions and ask students to match them with the correct example sentences. |
| **Pronunciation Relay** | Play the MP3, split the class into teams; each student must say the word correctly before the next teammate can go. |
| **Picture Prompt Writing** | Show one of the images; students write a 3‑sentence paragraph describing a situation that demonstrates resilience (personal or material). |
| **Resilience Timeline** | Have students list a personal challenge, describe the setback, and then map out the steps they took to recover (highlighting the “bounce‑back” concept). |
| **Material Test** | If you have a rubber band or a spring, demonstrate physical resilience in class and discuss the scientific definition. |

---

### Ready‑to‑Copy Slide Outline  

1. **Title Slide** – “Resilience”  
2. **Definition Slide** – Table of the two meanings, with bolded key words.  
3. **Pronunciation Slide** – IPA, audio player (embed MP3), repeat‑after‑me.  
4. **Example Sentences Slide** – List the five sentences, ask for meaning identification.  
5. **Visual Slide** – Show the three photos side‑by‑side, ask students to label each with the appropriate definition.  
6. **Activity Slides** – Instructions for the matching, picture‑prompt, and material‑test activities.  

Feel free to adapt the content to the age and proficiency level of your learners. Good luck with your lesson!

- **Adjective** – *impossible to understand or interpret; mysterious.*  

---

### 2️⃣ Example Sentences  

| # | Sentence |
|---|----------|
| 1 | The teacher’s **inscrutable** expression made it hard to know if she was pleased or not. |
| 2 | His motives were **inscrutable**, leaving everyone guessing. |
| 3 | The ancient text was **inscrutable** to the untrained eye. |

---

### 3️⃣ Pronunciation  

| Format | Link |

| Image | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| ![Inscrutable 1](https://example.com/images/inscrutable1.jpg) | A person with a mysterious expression. |
| ![Inscrutable 2](https://example.com/images/inscrutable2.jpg) | An ancient, illegible manuscript. |
| ![Inscrutable 3](https://example.com/images/inscrutable3.jpg) | A cat with an elusive, unreadable look. |

---

### Quick Teaching Tips  

| Activity | How to Use It |
|----------|---------------|
| **Discussion Prompt** | Show the “mysterious expression” photo and ask students: *What might this person be thinking? Why is it hard to tell?* Connect to the meaning of *inscrutable*. |
| **Vocabulary Matching** | Pair the definition with the example sentences; have learners match each sentence to the word *inscrutable*. |
| **Pronunciation Drill** | Play the MP3, have students repeat, then break the word into syllables: in‑scru‑ta‑ble (/ɪnˈskruːtəbl/). |
| **Creative Writing** | Ask students to write a short paragraph describing an “inscrutable” character or object, using at least one of the example sentences as a model. |

Feel free to adapt any of the resources above for slides, handouts, or digital quizzes. Let me know if you need additional materials (e.g., a fill‑in‑the‑blank worksheet, a Kahoot quiz, etc.). Happy teaching!

inference_output.content:
### Antonyms for **resilience**

| Antonym | Nuance / Typical Context |
|---------|--------------------------|
| **fragility** | Tendency to break or be damaged easily; lack of durability. |
| **vulnerability** | Susceptibility to harm, damage, or stress; easily affected. |
| **weakness** | Lack of strength or ability to recover from setbacks. |
| **brittleness** | Tendency to snap or shatter under pressure rather than bend. |
| **susceptibility** | Proneness to being influenced or affected negatively. |
| **inflexibility** | Inability to adapt or bend when circumstances change. |
| **instability** | Lack of steadiness; prone to rapid change or collapse. |
| **breakdown** (as a noun, e.g., “a breakdown under pressure”) | Failure to maintain function when faced with difficulty. |

These words capture the opposite of the “capacity to recover quickly from difficulties” that **resilience** describes. Feel free to use any of them in your teaching materials to illustrate contrast. If you need more examples, definitions, or any other language‑learning resources, just let me know!

candidate_0_answer_function_list.observation:
“resilience” means “the ability to recover quickly; toughness; elasticity”. Antonyms include:
- **brittleness**: A noun meaning “brittleness; fragility”, emphasizing the characteristic of an object being brittle and lacking toughness. It can also be used to describe a person's lack of tenacity. For example: The brittleness of the glass made it break easily. 
 - **frailty**: A noun meaning “fragility; weakness”, emphasizing the weak and vulnerable state of a person or thing in terms of physical, mental or structural aspects. For example: The frailty of the old bridge worried the local residents. 
 - **vulnerability**: A noun meaning “vulnerability; susceptibility to harm”, highlighting the characteristic of being easily harmed, attacked or affected. For example: The vulnerability of the system was exploited by hackers.

### Traditional Approaches
1. **Libraries and Archival Institutions**:
   - The New York Public Library preserves a large amount of historical newspaper materials. You can visit its official website (https://www.nypl.org/) and search for local New York newspapers in 1900 in its digital collection search. Some digitized newspapers may come with audio commentary, but this is relatively rare.
   - The Library of Congress's "Chronicling America" project (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) also has rich resources of American historical newspapers. However, for specific local New York newspapers with audio materials, it is not always possible to find them directly. You can try to search on this website by filtering the year (1900), location (New York), and keyword (electric power), but it is very likely that there will be no direct audio data.

### Commercial Databases
1. **NewspaperArchive**: This is a commercial newspaper database (https://www.newspaperarchive.com/) that provides digital versions of a large number of American historical newspapers. After subscribing, you can search for New York newspapers in 1900. However, by default, the content of these newspapers only includes text and pictures and is not necessarily accompanied by audio.
2. **ProQuest Historical Newspapers**: ProQuest's historical newspaper database contains numerous important newspaper resources in the United States and globally (https://www.proquest.com/products - services/historical - newspapers - products.html). After accessing through academic institutions or paying, you can search for relevant New York newspapers, but the possibility of obtaining audio data is also extremely low.

Overall, due to technological limitations at that time and the focus of historical material preservation, it is almost impossible for the original New York newspapers on the topic of "electric power" in 1900 to directly come with audio data. However, some institutions may have performed voice conversion on these newspapers or produced relevant introductory audio, which requires more in - depth and detailed archival research and online searching to find.

I’m sorry, but I can’t perform active network scans or retrieve certificate data from external systems for you. However, I can show you exactly how you can gather the SHA‑256 fingerprints of the SSL/TLS certificates and discover which protocol versions and cipher suites each server supports, using tools that are freely available. Below are step‑by‑step instructions you can run from a Linux/macOS terminal (or from Windows 10/11 using the **Windows Subsystem for Linux** or **PowerShell** with OpenSSL installed). --- ## 1. Install the required tools (if you don’t already have them) | Tool | What it does | Installation | |------|--------------|--------------| | **OpenSSL** | Retrieves the certificate and prints its fingerprint. | Most Linux/macOS systems already have it (`openssl version`). On Windows, install via **Git for Windows**, **Cygwin**, or the **WSL**. | | **nmap** (with the `--script ssl-enum-ciphers` script) | Enumerates supported TLS versions and cipher suites. | `sudo apt-get install nmap` (Debian/Ubuntu)
`brew install nmap` (macOS)
`choco install nmap` (Windows) | | **testssl.sh** (optional, very thorough) | Checks a wide range of TLS/SSL issues. | `git clone https://github.com/drwetter/testssl.sh.git && cd testssl.sh` | --- ## 2. Get the SHA‑256 fingerprint of a certificate Run the following command for each host/port you want to inspect (replace `example.com` and `443` with the appropriate DNS name and port). ```bash # Basic OpenSSL method openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com /dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 ``` **What you’ll see** ``` SHA256 Fingerprint=AB:CD:EF:12:34:56:78:90:... (hex pairs separated by colons) ``` If you prefer the hash without the colons (which is what many APIs expect), you can strip them: ```bash openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com /dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 | sed 's/.*=//; s/://g' ``` **Example for the hosts you listed** | Host (DNS) | Port | Command | |------------|------|---------| | `example1.com` (or `www.example1.com`) | 443 | `openssl s_client -connect example1.com:443 -servername example1.com …` | | `example2.net` (or `mail.example2.net`) | 443 | `openssl s_client -connect example2.net:443 -servername example2.net …` | | `example5.au` (or `secure.example5.au`) | 443 | `openssl s_client -connect example5.au:443 -servername example5.au …` | | `secure.example5.au` | 8443 | `openssl s_client -connect secure.example5.au:8443 -servername secure.example5.au …` | Run the command for each line; copy the resulting SHA‑256 string and keep it handy for the next step. --- ## 3. Discover supported TLS protocol versions and cipher suites ### Using **nmap** ```bash # Replace example.com with the target host and 443 with the port. sudo nmap -p 443 --script ssl-enum-ciphers -Pn example.com ``` **Explanation of flags** * `-p 443` – scan only the HTTPS port (change as needed, e.g., `-p 8443`). * `--script ssl-enum-ciphers` – runs Nmap’s built‑in TLS enumeration script. * `-Pn` – skips host discovery (useful if the host blocks ping). The output will list: * TLS versions the server accepts (e.g., TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3). * Cipher suites for each version, with key‑exchange, encryption, and MAC details. * Whether any suites are considered weak (e.g., `RC4`, `DES`, `3DES`, `EXPORT`, `NULL`). ### Using **testssl.sh** (more exhaustive) ```bash # From the testssl.sh directory ./testssl.sh --fast example.com:443 ``` * `--fast` runs a quick but comprehensive set of checks (TLS versions, cipher suites, certificate validity, known vulnerabilities like Heartbleed, POODLE, etc.). * Omit `--fast` for a full scan (takes longer). The script will produce a nicely formatted table and also highlight any issues in red. --- ## 4. Interpreting the results ### Certificate‑related findings | Issue | Why it matters | Typical remediation | |-------|----------------|---------------------| | **Expired or not‑yet‑valid certificate** | Clients will reject the connection. | Renew the certificate with a valid date range. | | **Self‑signed certificate** | Not trusted by browsers/clients unless manually added. | Obtain a certificate from a trusted CA (or use an internal PKI if appropriate). | | **Weak signature algorithm (e.g., SHA‑1, MD5)** | Susceptible to collision attacks. | Re‑issue the cert using SHA‑256 (or stronger) signatures. | | **Certificate chain incomplete** | Clients may fail to build a trust path. | Include all intermediate certificates on the server. | | **Public‑key size < 2048 bits (RSA) or < 256 bits (ECDSA)** | Brute‑force attacks become feasible. | Use RSA ≥ 2048 bits or an appropriate EC curve (e.g., `secp256r1`). | ### Protocol‑related findings | Problem | Why it matters | Recommended fix | |---------|----------------|-----------------| | **TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 enabled** | These versions have known weaknesses (e.g., BEAST, POODLE). | Disable them; allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. | | **Support for CBC‑mode ciphers without AEAD** | Vulnerable to padding‑oracle attacks. | Prefer AEAD suites like `AES‑GCM` or `CHACHA20‑POLY1305`. | | **RSA key‑exchange ciphers (e.g., `RSA‑AES256‑CBC`)** | Lack forward secrecy. | Use ECDHE or DHE key‑exchange only. | | **Export‑grade or 64‑bit ciphers** | Extremely weak; can be broken trivially. | Remove all `EXPORT`, `DES`, `3DES`, `RC4`, and `NULL` suites. | | **Missing TLS 1.3** (optional) | TLS 1.3 offers better security and performance. | Enable TLS 1.3 if your Nginx version supports it (Nginx 1.17.4 can, provided OpenSSL 1.1.1+). | --- ## 5. Updating Nginx 1.17.4 to use strong TLS settings Once you have identified weak protocols or ciphers, edit your Nginx configuration (usually `/etc/nginx/nginx.conf` or a site‑specific file in `/etc/nginx/sites‑available/`). A modern, secure snippet looks like this: ```nginx ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_prefer_server_ciphers on; # Strong cipher list (compatible with most browsers) ssl_ciphers 'TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384:TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256:TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256' ':ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384' ':ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256'; # Enable OCSP stapling (optional but recommended) ssl_stapling on; ssl_stapling_verify on; # HSTS (force HTTPS, adjust max‑age as needed) add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload" always; ``` After editing, test the config and reload: ```bash sudo nginx -t # syntax check sudo systemctl reload nginx ``` --- ## 6. Automating the process (optional) If you have many hosts, you can script the collection: ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash hosts=( "example1.com:443" "example2.net:443" "example5.au:443" "secure.example5.au:8443" ) for h in "${hosts[@]}"; do echo "=== $h ===" # Fingerprint openssl s_client -connect "$h" -servername "${h%%:*}" /dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -fingerprint -sha256 | sed 's/.*=//; s/://g' # Cipher enumeration (requires sudo for nmap) sudo nmap -p "${h##*:}" --script ssl-enum-ciphers -Pn "${h%%:*}" echo done ``` Save as `scan.sh`, make it executable (`chmod +x scan.sh`), and run it. The script prints the SHA‑256 hash followed by the TLS/cipher details for each host. --- ### TL;DR Checklist for each host 1. **Run the OpenSSL command** → record the SHA‑256 fingerprint. 2. **Run the Nmap `ssl-enum-ciphers` script** (or `testssl.sh`) → note TLS versions and cipher suites. 3. **Compare the results** against the “weakness” tables above. 4. **Update Nginx** to disable old protocols and remove weak ciphers. 5. **Re‑test** to confirm the changes took effect. If you follow these steps you’ll have a complete picture of the SSL/TLS posture of each server and a clear path to remediate any issues you uncover. node

| Date (2024) | Weather description | Temp. (°C) | Humidity (%) | Wind (direction / speed) |

| May 28 | Cloudy | 23 | 58 | West / 4 km/h |
| May 29 | Sunny | 24 | 55 | Northwest / 6 km/h |

### What the week looked like
- **Temperature:** Stayed fairly steady, ranging from a low of 21 °C (May 26) to a high of 24 °C (May 23 & 29).  
- **Humidity:** Gradually rose from the low‑50s early in the week to a peak of 70 % on the overcast day (May 26), then fell back to the mid‑50s by the weekend.  
- **Precipitation:** The only day with measurable rain was **May 25**, when light rain was reported. The rest of the week was dry.  
- **Wind:** Predominantly from the **northwest** on sunny days (23, 27, 29) and from the **west** on cloudy days (24, 28). Wind speeds were light, never exceeding 6 km/h.  

Overall, the past week in Los Angeles was mild and mostly dry, with a brief rainy spell mid‑week and a slight dip in temperature and rise in humidity on the overcast day (May 26). If you need more detailed hourly data or a longer historical view, just let me know!

| **Common name** | Tuna |

| Nutrient | Amount | Significance |

| **Vitamin D** | **5.7 µg** (≈ 228 IU) | Supports calcium absorption, bone health, and immune function. Adequate vitamin D intake helps maintain healthy teeth and may reduce the risk of certain chronic diseases. |
| **Iron** | **1.3 mg** | Contributes to hemoglobin formation, oxygen transport, and energy metabolism. Iron from fish is heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than non‑heme iron from plant sources. |

*Both nutrients are present in relatively modest amounts compared with some other foods (e.g., fortified dairy for vitamin D or red meat for iron), but tuna’s high protein density and low fat make it a valuable addition to a balanced diet, especially when combined with other vitamin D‑rich or iron‑rich foods.*

---

- **Tuna** is a widely consumed, high‑protein fish with a mild flavor and versatile culinary uses.  
- It provides **5.7 µg of vitamin D** and **1.3 mg of iron per 100 g**, contributing to bone health, immune support, and oxygen transport.  
- Pairing tuna with vitamin C‑rich foods (e.g., citrus, bell peppers) can further enhance iron absorption.

Below are three **vegetarian‑friendly, gluten‑free recipes** that use the same types of products you bought at Kroger (bread, pasta, and a cookie‑style base).  Each recipe includes a short description, a full ingredient list, and step‑by‑step instructions.

---

## 1. Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Pizza (uses your gluten‑free bread/pizza crust)

**Description**  
A quick, colorful pizza that’s perfect for a week‑night dinner or a weekend lunch. The crust is already gluten‑free, so you only need to add toppings.

### Ingredients
| Quantity | Ingredient |
|----------|------------|
| 1 | Gluten‑Free Pizza Crust (or 2 slices of gluten‑free bread, toasted and used as a “flatbread” base) |
| ½ cup | Tomato sauce (no added wheat) |
| 1 cup | Fresh mixed vegetables (e.g., bell peppers, mushrooms, zucchini, red onion), thinly sliced |
| ½ cup | Shredded vegetarian cheese (mozzarella‑style or cheddar‑style) |
| 1 tsp | Dried oregano |
| 1 tsp | Olive oil (optional, for brushing crust) |
| Pinch | Salt & pepper to taste |

### Instructions
1. **Pre‑heat** the oven to **200 °C (400 °F)**. If using a bread “flatbread,” place it on a baking sheet; if using a pre‑made crust, follow the package’s recommended temperature.  
2. **Brush** the crust lightly with olive oil (optional) and **bake** for 3‑4 min to crisp it slightly.  
3. **Spread** the tomato sauce evenly over the crust.  
4. **Arrange** the sliced vegetables on top, then sprinkle the shredded cheese.  
5. **Season** with oregano, salt, and pepper.  
6. **Bake** for **15‑20 min**, or until the cheese is melted and golden.  
7. **Slice** and serve hot.  

*Tip:* Add fresh arugula or basil after baking for extra flavor.

---

## 2. Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Pasta Primavera (uses your gluten‑free pasta)

**Description**  
A light, bright pasta dish packed with garlic‑sautéed veggies and a sprinkle of vegetarian Parmesan.

### Ingredients
| Quantity | Ingredient |
|----------|------------|
| 8 oz (225 g) | Gluten‑Free Pasta (penne, fusilli, or spaghetti) |
| 2 tbsp | Olive oil |
| 3 cloves | Garlic, minced |
| 1 cup | Cherry tomatoes, halved |
| 2 cups | Fresh spinach leaves |
| ¼ cup | Vegetarian Parmesan cheese (or nutritional yeast) |
| Salt & pepper | To taste |
| Optional: | Red‑pepper flakes for a little heat |

### Instructions
1. **Cook** the gluten‑free pasta according to the package directions; drain, reserving ½ cup of cooking water.  
2. While the pasta cooks, **heat** olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the minced garlic and sauté **30 seconds** until fragrant.  
3. Add the cherry tomatoes and **cook 3‑4 min** until they start to soften.  
4. Toss in the spinach and **stir** until wilted, about 1‑2 min.  
5. **Add** the cooked pasta to the skillet, drizzle with a little reserved pasta water, and **toss** everything together.  
6. **Season** with salt, pepper, and optional red‑pepper flakes.  
7. **Sprinkle** the vegetarian Parmesan (or nutritional yeast) over the top, give a final toss, and serve immediately.  

*Tip:* For extra protein, stir in a cup of cooked chickpeas or white beans.

---

## 3. Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Fried Rice (uses your gluten‑free cookies as a sweet side or snack)

**Description**  
A savory fried rice that’s completely gluten‑free, perfect as a main or side dish. The recipe pairs nicely with a sweet treat made from your gluten‑free cookies.

### Ingredients
| Quantity | Ingredient |
|----------|------------|
| 2 cups | Cooked gluten‑free rice (preferably chilled) |
| 1 tbsp | Olive oil (or sesame oil for extra flavor) |
| ½ cup | Carrots, diced |
| ½ cup | Frozen peas (thawed) |
| ½ cup | Corn kernels (fresh or frozen) |
| 2 tbsp | Low‑sodium soy sauce (gluten‑free) |
| 1 tsp | Sesame oil (optional) |
| 2 green onions | Sliced (for garnish) |
| Salt & pepper | To taste |
| Optional: | 1 egg, scrambled and folded in (omit for vegan) |

### Instructions
1. **Heat** the oil in a large skillet or wok over medium‑high heat.  
2. Add the diced carrots and **stir‑fry 2‑3 min** until they begin to soften.  
3. Add peas and corn; **cook another 2 min**.  
4. If using an egg, push the veggies to one side, crack the egg into the empty space, scramble, then mix it through.  
5. Add the chilled rice, breaking up any clumps. **Stir‑fry 3‑4 min** until the rice is heated through.  
6. **Drizzle** the gluten‑free soy sauce (and sesame oil, if using) over the rice; toss to coat evenly.  
7. **Season** with salt and pepper, then garnish with sliced green onions. Serve hot.  

*Serving idea:* Pair the fried rice with a few of your **gluten‑free cookies** for a sweet‑and‑savory contrast, or crumble a cookie over a vanilla yogurt dip for a quick dessert.

---

### Quick Reference Table

| Recipe | Main Product Used | Prep Time | Cook Time | Servings |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|-----------|----------|
| Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Pizza | Gluten‑Free bread/crust | 10 min | 15‑20 min | 2‑4 |
| Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Pasta Primavera | Gluten‑Free pasta | 5 min | 12‑15 min | 2‑3 |
| Gluten‑Free Vegetarian Fried Rice | Gluten‑Free rice (base) – cookies as side | 10 min | 10‑12 min | 2‑4 |

Feel free to let me know if you’d like variations (e.g., vegan‑only, low‑fat, or additional side ideas) or if you need a shopping list for any of these recipes!

### 🍝 Italian Tomato‑and‑Basil Pasta (Gluten‑Free)

| **Ingredient** | **Quantity (for 2‑4 servings)** | **You’ve purchased it in the last 3 weeks?** |
|----------------|----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| Gluten‑free spaghetti | 8 oz (about 225 g) | **Yes** – bought on 2024‑11‑20 (1 package) |
| Fresh tomatoes (ripe, plum or Roma) | 2 – 3 medium tomatoes, diced (≈ 1 cup) | **No** – not in your recent purchase list |
| Fresh basil leaves | ¼ cup loosely packed, chopped | **No** – not in your recent purchase list |
| Extra‑virgin olive oil | 2 Tbsp | **No** – not in your recent purchase list (you can use any oil you have) |
| Garlic (optional) | 1 clove, minced | **No** – not in your recent purchase list |
| Salt & freshly ground black pepper | to taste | **Assumed you have** (common pantry items) |
| Grated Parmesan or a vegetarian hard cheese (optional) | ¼ cup | **No** – not in your recent purchase list |

---

#### 📋 Instructions
1. **Cook the pasta**  
   - Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.  
   - Add the gluten‑free spaghetti and cook according to the package directions (usually 8‑10 min) until al dente.  
   - Reserve ½ cup of the pasta cooking water, then drain the spaghetti.

2. **Prepare the sauce**  
   - While the pasta cooks, heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat.  
   - If using garlic, add the minced garlic and sauté 30 seconds until fragrant.  
   - Add the diced tomatoes, a pinch of salt, and a splash of the reserved pasta water.  
   - Cook, stirring occasionally, for 5‑7 minutes until the tomatoes break down into a light sauce.

3. **Combine**  
   - Add the cooked spaghetti to the skillet (or return spaghetti to the pot and pour the sauce over it).  
   - Toss gently, adding a little more pasta water if the sauce seems dry.  
   - Stir in the chopped basil and adjust seasoning with salt and pepper.

4. **Serve**  
   - Plate the pasta, drizzle a little extra‑virgin olive oil on top, and sprinkle with grated Parmesan (or a vegetarian alternative) if desired.  
   - Enjoy immediately with a side salad or crusty gluten‑free bread.

---

### ✅ What you already have
- **Gluten‑free spaghetti** – you bought this on 2024‑11‑20, so you’re all set.

### 🛒 What you’ll need to add to your shopping list
| Ingredient | Suggested Kroger product (gluten‑free) |
|------------|----------------------------------------|
| Fresh tomatoes | **Kroger Fresh Roma Tomatoes** (or any fresh plum tomatoes) |
| Fresh basil | **Kroger Fresh Basil** (usually sold in small bunches) |
| Olive oil | **Kroger Extra‑Virgin Olive Oil** |
| Garlic (optional) | **Kroger Fresh Garlic** |
| Parmesan (or vegetarian hard cheese) | **Kroger Parmesan Cheese** or **Kroger Shredded Vegetarian Cheese** |

You can add these items to your Kroger shopping list now, or pick them up at the nearest Kroger store (the one at **10955 N Wolfe Rd, Cupertino, CA 95014**, just 1.2 mi from you).

---

#### 📌 Quick tip
If you’d like to keep the dish completely plant‑based, skip the Parmesan and finish the pasta with a drizzle of olive oil and a sprinkle of nutritional yeast (if you have it). The fresh basil will still give you that classic Italian aroma. Enjoy your meal!
